title: Grade 5
emphasis: Flexible meanings and common academic language

words.definition: to figure out and explain what something means

hero.text: Pixel studied the strange symbols on the ancient map and tried to interpret what each mark meant for the team.

words.everyday: Our class worked together to interpret the poem, deciding that the storm stood for the speaker's anger.

contrast.nonExample: Jonah copied the poem word for word into his notebook without thinking about it.
contrast.explanation: Copying words is not interpreting. To interpret, you have to decide what the words or signs actually mean.

items.prompt: What does "interpret" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Scientists interpret the rings inside a tree trunk to learn how much rain fell in each year of its life.

options.text: to figure out what something means
to draw a copy of something

items.hint: The scientists look at the rings in order to learn something. What are they doing with the rings?
items.explanation: The scientists use the rings "to learn how much rain fell". They are working out what the rings mean, which is what interpret means.

wrong.a: Counting rings tells the tree's age, but the sentence is about what the rings tell us about rain.
wrong.b: Nothing in the sentence is about cutting.
wrong.d: Copying the rings would not explain anything about rain.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The bar graph was confusing at first, so Ms. Lee showed us how to ___ the height of each bar.
items.clue: confusing at first; showed us how
items.hint: The graph was confusing. What would the teacher help students do with it?
items.explanation: Because the graph was "confusing at first", the teacher helped students understand what each bar means. That is interpreting the graph.

wrong.b: Decorating a graph would not make it less confusing.
wrong.c: The teacher wanted students to understand the bars, not ignore them.
wrong.d: Measuring gives a number, but the problem was understanding what the bars meant.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "interpret" in this sentence?
items.passage: Ancient sailors learned to interpret the shapes of clouds as signs that a storm was coming.
items.hint: The sailors looked at clouds and understood them as signs. Which word can mean understanding signs?
items.explanation: Here, "read" means understanding signs, like reading the sky. The sailors understood the cloud shapes as warnings, which is interpreting them.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what interpret means.

chunks.text: In art class, we tried to interpret
the painting's dark colors
as a sign of sadness.
by hanging it on the wall.

items.hint: Interpreting means deciding what something means. Which ending tells a meaning?
items.explanation: "As a sign of sadness" explains what the colors mean, so it shows interpreting. Hanging a painting on a wall does not explain its meaning.

items.prompt: Which word best describes what Amir did?
items.passage: When his grandmother nodded slowly and smiled, Amir decided her look meant she was proud of his science project.
items.clue: decided her look meant
items.hint: Amir looked at a nod and a smile and decided what they meant.
items.explanation: "Decided her look meant" shows Amir figured out the meaning of his grandmother's expression. That is interpreting. Interrupted sounds similar but means cutting someone off.

wrong.c: Interrupted looks similar, but it means breaking in while someone is talking.

words.definition: large in amount, size, or importance

hero.text: Rex lifted a substantial pile of fallen bricks off the road so the families could finally drive home.

words.everyday: The library received a substantial donation that paid for hundreds of new books and three computers.

contrast.nonExample: Tia found a single penny on the sidewalk and put it in her pocket.
contrast.explanation: One penny is a tiny amount. Substantial describes something large enough to really matter.

items.prompt: Is this an example of something substantial?
items.passage: After a week of dry weather, the town reservoir rose by only half an inch, barely enough to notice.
items.hint: Is half an inch, barely enough to notice, a large amount?
items.explanation: Half an inch that is "barely enough to notice" is a tiny amount. Substantial means large in amount or importance, so this does not fit.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Our bake sale earned ___ profits this year, more than enough to pay for the whole class trip.
items.clue: more than enough to pay for the whole class trip
items.hint: How much money would pay for a whole trip with some left over?
items.explanation: "More than enough to pay for the whole class trip" shows the amount was large. Substantial fits. Tiny is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is the OPPOSITE of "substantial" in this sentence?
items.passage: The new medicine caused a substantial drop in fevers among the patients in the study.
items.hint: Substantial means large. Which word means very small?
items.explanation: Slight means small, the opposite of substantial. Major means almost the same as substantial. Sudden is about speed, not size.

items.prompt: Which word fits best?
items.passage: Building the new bridge will take a ___ effort: two years of work and hundreds of workers.
items.clue: two years of work and hundreds of workers
items.hint: Look at the details after the colon. Is this a big job or a little one?
items.explanation: "Two years" and "hundreds of workers" describe a very large effort. Substantial fits. Quick and small contradict those details.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the meal?
items.passage: Before the long hike, Dad cooked a hearty breakfast of eggs, oatmeal, and fruit that kept us full until dinner.
items.clue: hearty; kept us full until dinner
items.hint: A meal that keeps you full all day must be big. Which word describes that?
items.explanation: "Hearty" and "kept us full until dinner" show the breakfast was large and filling. That is substantial. Skimpy means too small.

words.definition: to notice or show the difference between things

hero.text: Juniper could distinguish the real robot from its copy because the real one had a tiny scratch on its arm.

words.everyday: Good readers learn to distinguish facts, which can be checked, from opinions, which tell what someone believes.

contrast.nonExample: Leo dumped all the red and blue beads into one jar without looking at them.
contrast.explanation: Mixing things together without noticing what makes them different is not distinguishing. Distinguishing means telling things apart.

items.prompt: Which student is able to distinguish between two things?

options.text: Nia thinks frogs and toads are exactly the same animal.
Omar draws a frog and colors it bright green.
Lily knows toads have bumpy, dry skin and frogs have smooth, wet skin.
Sam reads a short story about a frog prince.

items.hint: Distinguish means telling the difference. Who can tell frogs and toads apart?
items.explanation: Lily names the difference between toads and frogs, so she can distinguish them. Nia mixes them up, which is the opposite.

wrong.a: Nia mixes the animals up, so she cannot distinguish them.
wrong.b: Drawing one frog does not compare two things.
wrong.d: Reading a story does not show telling things apart.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The twins look so alike that even their teacher cannot ___ one from the other without their name tags.
items.clue: look so alike; one from the other
items.hint: When two people look alike, what is hard to do?
items.explanation: "Look so alike" and "one from the other" signal telling two things apart. The teacher cannot distinguish the twins.

wrong.c: Remember does not fit with "one from the other". The problem is telling them apart.

items.prompt: Which phrase is closest in meaning to "distinguish" in this sentence?
items.passage: Bats use echoes to distinguish a moth from a leaf, even in total darkness.
items.hint: The bat needs to know which object is food and which is not.
items.explanation: To distinguish a moth from a leaf is to tell them apart. Chasing comes later, after the bat knows which one is the moth.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what distinguish means.

chunks.text: A trained ear can distinguish
a violin from a viola
by the deeper sound of the viola.
because both sound exactly the same.

items.hint: To distinguish, you need a difference to notice.
items.explanation: "The deeper sound of the viola" is the difference that lets you tell them apart. If both sounded exactly the same, you could not distinguish them.

items.prompt: Which line uses "distinguish" correctly?

options.text: "Please distinguish the lights so we can sleep."
"I distinguish pizza more than any other food."
"He will distinguish his homework by Friday."
"Can you distinguish a crow from a raven?"

items.hint: Which line is about telling two similar things apart?
items.explanation: Crows and ravens look alike, so asking if someone can distinguish them means asking if they can tell them apart. Option a confuses distinguish with extinguish, which means put out.

wrong.a: This mixes up distinguish with extinguish (to put out a light or fire).
wrong.b: This should be a word like enjoy or prefer.
wrong.c: This should be a word like finish.

words.definition: continuing to try or to happen, even when it is hard

hero.text: Kai was persistent, rebuilding his glider again and again until it finally soared across the training field.

words.everyday: Marie Curie was persistent, spending years of careful work to discover two new chemical elements.

contrast.nonExample: Ella tried one hard puzzle, got stuck after a minute, and put it back on the shelf.
contrast.explanation: Giving up quickly is the opposite of being persistent. A persistent person keeps going when something is difficult.

items.prompt: Is this person persistent?
items.passage: Marco failed his swim test once, said swimming wasn't for him, and never went back to the pool.
items.hint: Did Marco keep trying after it got hard?
items.explanation: Marco stopped after one failure. A persistent person keeps trying even when something is hard, so this does not fit.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The ___ cough lasted for three weeks, so Grandpa finally went to the doctor to get it checked.
items.clue: lasted for three weeks
items.hint: This time the word describes a cough, not a person. What kind of cough lasts for weeks?
items.explanation: "Lasted for three weeks" shows the cough kept happening. Persistent can describe something that continues for a long time, not just a person who keeps trying.

wrong.b: Sudden means it started quickly, but the clue is about how long it lasted.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "persistent" in this sentence?
items.passage: The persistent reporter called the mayor's office every day until she finally got an interview.
items.hint: She called every day until she succeeded. What quality does that show?
items.explanation: Determined means refusing to give up, which matches calling "every day until" she got the interview. Rude adds a bad attitude the sentence never mentions.

items.prompt: "Persistent" comes from "persist" plus the suffix -ent. If "persist" means to keep going, what does "persistent" mean?
items.hint: The suffix -ent turns a verb into a describing word: someone or something that does the action.
items.explanation: -ent means having the quality of doing the action. Persist means keep going, so persistent describes something that keeps on going.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the woodpecker?
items.passage: All morning the woodpecker tapped at the same tree, ignoring the wind and rain, until it had carved a deep hole.
items.clue: All morning; ignoring the wind and rain; until
items.hint: The bird kept working through bad weather. What word describes that?
items.explanation: "All morning", "ignoring the wind and rain", and "until" show the woodpecker kept going despite difficulty. That is persistent.

words.definition: existing in large amounts; more than enough

hero.text: Juniper's garden was so abundant that the academy had enough tomatoes and beans to share with the whole neighborhood.

words.everyday: Rainforests have abundant rainfall, which helps thousands of kinds of plants grow there.

contrast.nonExample: In the desert, water is so scarce that plants must store every drop they can find.
contrast.explanation: Scarce means there is too little. Abundant means there is plenty, more than enough.

items.prompt: What does "abundant" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Fish were so abundant in the river that the bears could catch dinner in just a few minutes.
items.hint: If bears catch fish in a few minutes, are there many fish or few?
items.explanation: Bears catching dinner "in just a few minutes" shows there were plenty of fish. Abundant means existing in large amounts.

wrong.a: This is the opposite: scarce. Easy catching shows there were many fish.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Oil was ___ in that region a century ago, but after years of drilling, very little is left.
items.clue: but; very little is left
items.hint: "But" signals a change. Now very little is left, so what was it like before?
items.explanation: "But" sets up a contrast with "very little is left", so oil must once have been plentiful. Abundant fits. Scarce describes now, not a century ago.

wrong.c: Scarce describes the situation now. "But" tells you the past was the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "abundant" in this sentence?
items.passage: After the spring rains, wildflowers were abundant across the hills, covering them in purple and gold.
items.hint: The flowers covered the hills. Were there a lot of them?
items.explanation: Plentiful means there is a lot, just like abundant. "Covering them" shows how many flowers there were.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what abundant means.

chunks.text: Apples were abundant this fall,
so every family in town
had to share just one basket.
could pick as many as they wanted.

items.hint: If something is abundant, is there a shortage or plenty?
items.explanation: Abundant means there is more than enough, so families "could pick as many as they wanted". Sharing one basket shows a shortage, the opposite of abundant.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the food in the forest?
items.passage: In autumn, acorns, berries, and seeds covered the forest floor, giving squirrels far more food than they could ever eat.
items.clue: covered the forest floor; far more food than they could ever eat
items.hint: Look for the words that tell how much food there was.
items.explanation: "Covered the forest floor" and "far more food than they could ever eat" show there was plenty. That is abundant. Rare is the opposite.

words.definition: to change in order to fit a new situation or place

hero.text: When the power went out, Bolt had to adapt quickly, using flashlights instead of screens to guide the rescue team.

words.everyday: Arctic foxes adapt to the seasons by growing thick white fur in winter and thinner brown fur in summer.

contrast.nonExample: Even after moving to a hot city, Ben kept wearing his heavy winter coat every day.
contrast.explanation: Ben did not change to fit his new place. To adapt, you change to suit a new situation.

items.prompt: Is this an example of adapting?
items.passage: When the soccer field flooded, the coach moved practice into the gym and changed the drills to fit the smaller space.
items.hint: Did the coach change the plan to fit a new situation?
items.explanation: The coach changed both the place and the drills to fit the new situation. Changing to fit new conditions is adapting.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Camels ___ to the dry desert by storing fat in their humps and going days without drinking water.
items.clue: storing fat; going days without drinking
items.hint: The sentence lists ways camels' bodies fit their dry home.
items.explanation: Storing fat and going days without water are ways camels are suited to the desert. They adapt to it. Escape would mean leaving the desert.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "adapt" in this sentence?
items.passage: It took a few weeks for Rosa to adapt to her new school, but now she has friends in every class.
items.hint: Rosa needed time to get used to something new.
items.explanation: Adjust means to get used to something new, which matches adapt. "It took a few weeks" shows Rosa slowly fit in.

items.prompt: Which word fits best?
items.passage: The author decided to ___ the long novel into a short play that her students could perform in one hour.
items.clue: into a short play; in one hour
items.hint: Adapt means to change something to fit. Adopt means to take something as your own.
items.explanation: The author changed the novel to fit a new form, so adapt fits. Adopt looks similar but means to take on or take in, like adopting a pet.

wrong.b: Adopt means to take something as your own. The author is changing the story, not taking it.

items.prompt: What did the city do?
items.passage: As summers grew hotter, the city planted shade trees, opened cooling centers, and moved outdoor events to the evening.
items.clue: planted shade trees; opened cooling centers; moved outdoor events
items.hint: Each action is a change that helps people handle hotter summers.
items.explanation: Planting trees, opening cooling centers, and moving events are changes made to fit hotter weather. That is adapting.

words.definition: to study something closely, part by part, to understand it

hero.text: Pixel analyzed the footprints one by one, measuring their size and depth to figure out who had crossed the mud.

words.everyday: In science class, we analyzed soil samples by testing each one for water, sand, and tiny living things.

contrast.nonExample: Max glanced at the chart for a second and said, "Looks fine," before moving on.
contrast.explanation: A quick glance is not analyzing. To analyze, you look closely at each part to understand how it works.

items.prompt: Which student is analyzing?

options.text: Kim reads the story's title and closes the book.
Ravi studies each scene to see why the main character changes.
Jada guesses the ending without reading.
Theo hands the book to a friend.

items.hint: Analyzing means looking closely at parts to understand something.
items.explanation: Ravi studies "each scene" to understand why the character changes. Looking closely at parts to understand the whole is analyzing.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Before choosing a new lunch menu, the school will ___ the survey results to see which foods students like most.
items.clue: to see which foods students like most
items.hint: The school wants to learn something from the results. What must it do with them?
items.explanation: To find out "which foods students like most", the school must study the results closely. That is analyzing.

wrong.b: Printing the results would not tell the school which foods are most popular.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "analyzed" in this sentence?
items.passage: The detective analyzed every clue, from the muddy boots to the torn letter, before naming a suspect.
items.hint: The detective looked closely at each clue to reach an answer.
items.explanation: Examined means looked at carefully, which matches analyzed. Collected means gathered, but analyzing is studying what you gathered.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what analyze means.

chunks.text: The coach analyzed the game video
play by play
to find where the defense made mistakes.
without paying attention to any details.

items.hint: Analyzing means paying close attention to details.
items.explanation: Going "play by play" to find mistakes shows close study of parts. Ignoring details is the opposite of analyzing.

items.prompt: Which line uses "analyze" naturally?

options.text: "Let's analyze outside before the bell rings."
"I analyzed my sandwich in two bites."
"We should analyze the water samples to see why the fish got sick."
"Analyze me a glass of juice, please."

items.hint: Which speaker wants to study something closely to understand it?
items.explanation: Studying water samples to find out why fish got sick is close study to understand a problem. That is analyzing. The other lines use the word like play, eat, or pour.

words.definition: to expect something and get ready for it before it happens

hero.text: Nova anticipated the rockslide, so she moved the hikers off the trail minutes before the boulders tumbled down.

words.everyday: The museum anticipated large crowds for the dinosaur exhibit, so it hired extra guides for the weekend.

contrast.nonExample: The storm surprised everyone at the picnic, and nobody had brought an umbrella.
contrast.explanation: Being caught by surprise is the opposite of anticipating. To anticipate, you expect something and prepare ahead of time.

items.prompt: Is this an example of anticipating?
items.passage: Mr. Patel forgot about the fire drill, so his class was in the middle of a test when the alarm rang.
items.hint: Did Mr. Patel expect the drill and get ready for it?
items.explanation: Mr. Patel forgot about the drill, so he did not expect it or prepare. Anticipating means expecting something and getting ready before it happens.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Good chess players ___ their opponent's next move and plan their own response before it happens.
items.clue: next move; before it happens
items.hint: The players think ahead about something that has not happened yet.
items.explanation: "Before it happens" shows the players expect the move and prepare for it. That is anticipating.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "anticipate" in this sentence?
items.passage: Farmers anticipate a dry summer, so they are digging new wells and storing extra water now.
items.hint: The dry summer has not happened yet, but the farmers think it will.
items.explanation: Expect means to think something will happen, which matches anticipate. Prevent would mean stopping the dry summer, which farmers cannot do.

items.prompt: The prefix "anti-" in "anticipate" comes from a Latin word meaning "before". How does that help explain the word?

options.text: It means to be against something.
It means to look back at the past.
It means to think about something before it happens.

items.hint: In this word, the beginning means "before", not "against".
items.explanation: Here, "anti-" means before, so anticipate means taking hold of an idea before the event comes. It is a trick: anti- in antifreeze means against, but not in anticipate.

wrong.a: Anti- often means against, as in antifreeze, but in anticipate it comes from a word meaning before.

items.prompt: Which word best describes what the bakery did?
items.passage: Knowing the town parade would bring hungry visitors, the bakery baked twice as many muffins the night before.
items.clue: Knowing; the night before
items.hint: The bakery got ready for something before it happened.
items.explanation: "Knowing" the visitors would come and baking "the night before" show the bakery expected the crowd and prepared. That is anticipating.

words.definition: to decide something is true after thinking about the evidence

hero.text: After seeing the open window and the wet paw prints, Juniper concluded that the cat had slipped outside in the rain.

words.everyday: After testing the plants for three weeks, the class concluded that the ones near the window grew fastest.

contrast.nonExample: Without looking at any data, Eli announced that his team's plant would win.
contrast.explanation: Eli guessed without evidence. To conclude, you decide what is true after thinking about the evidence.

items.prompt: What does "concluded" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The scientists studied the bones carefully and concluded that they came from a dinosaur that ate only plants.
items.hint: The scientists studied first, then decided something.
items.explanation: "Studied the bones carefully" is the evidence, and then they decided what was true. That is concluding. In other sentences, conclude can also mean to end, like "the concert concluded at nine", but here it means to decide.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Since every student who slept more scored higher, the researchers ___ that sleep helps memory.
items.clue: Since every student who slept more scored higher
items.hint: "Since" gives the evidence. What did the researchers do with it?
items.explanation: "Since" introduces the evidence, and the researchers used it to decide something was true. That is concluding. Wondered means they were still unsure.

wrong.a: Wondered means still asking a question, but the evidence led them to a decision.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what conclude means.

chunks.text: Because the ice melted fastest in the sun,
we concluded
that heat speeds up melting.
that we should never test anything.

items.hint: A conclusion should match the evidence that came before it.
items.explanation: Ice melting fastest in the sun is evidence that heat speeds up melting, so that is a sensible conclusion. The decoy does not follow from the evidence.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "concluded" in this sentence?
items.passage: After counting the votes twice, the class concluded that the field trip would be to the aquarium.
items.hint: They counted twice, so they were sure. Which word means finding out for sure?
items.explanation: Determined means figured out for sure, which matches concluded after counting twice. Guessed means deciding without enough evidence.

items.prompt: What can Zara reasonably conclude?
items.passage: Zara's bike tire is flat. She finds a sharp nail stuck in the rubber and hears air hissing out around it.

options.text: The nail made a hole in the tire.

items.clue: sharp nail stuck in the rubber; air hissing out
items.hint: Use the evidence: a nail and hissing air.
items.explanation: The nail stuck in the tire and the hissing air are evidence that the nail made a hole. To conclude is to decide what the evidence shows.

words.definition: to make someone believe something or agree to do something

hero.text: Bolt showed the mayor photos of the cracked dam and convinced her to send repair crews right away.

words.everyday: Lena used facts about plastic pollution to convince her class to start a recycling program.

contrast.nonExample: Amy told her brother to recycle, but he shrugged and kept throwing bottles in the trash.
contrast.explanation: Amy tried, but her brother did not change his mind. To convince, you must actually get someone to believe or agree.

items.prompt: Did Noah convince his parents?
items.passage: Noah explained how he would feed and walk a puppy every day, and his parents finally agreed to adopt one.
items.hint: Did his parents change their minds and agree?
items.explanation: Noah's reasons made his parents agree. Getting someone to believe or agree is what convince means.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The lawyer used fingerprints and a video to ___ the jury that her client was innocent.
items.clue: used fingerprints and a video; that her client was innocent
items.hint: She used evidence to make the jury believe something.
items.explanation: The lawyer used evidence to make the jury believe her client was innocent. That is convincing. Remind would mean the jury already knew it.

wrong.a: Remind means helping someone remember something they already knew.
wrong.d: Confusing the jury would not help them believe anything.

items.prompt: Which word fits best?
items.passage: Leo begged his sister for an hour to trade lunches, but he could not ___ her, so she kept her sandwich.
items.clue: begged for an hour; she kept her sandwich
items.hint: Leo did ask, but what didn't he manage to do?
items.explanation: Leo asked many times, so "could not ask" makes no sense. He failed to get her to agree, so "could not convince" fits. Convincing means succeeding at changing a mind.

wrong.b: Leo did ask, for an hour. What failed was changing her mind.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "convince" in this sentence?
items.passage: Our posters helped convince the town council to build a new skate park near the library.
items.hint: The posters gave reasons that changed the council's minds.
items.explanation: Persuade means to get someone to agree by giving reasons, which matches convince. Force and trick are not about honest reasons.

items.prompt: Which line uses "convince" correctly?

options.text: "I convinced the ball over the fence."
"The data convinced me that bees are important."

items.hint: Convince is about changing what someone believes.
items.explanation: The data changed what the speaker believes about bees, so it convinced them. The other lines use convince like kick, pass, or bloom.

words.definition: to prepare land and grow crops or plants on it

hero.text: Juniper helped the villagers cultivate the rocky hillside, clearing stones and planting rows of corn and squash.

words.everyday: Ancient Egyptians cultivated wheat along the Nile, where yearly floods left rich soil behind.

contrast.nonExample: Wild blackberries grew along the fence without anyone planting or watering them.
contrast.explanation: Plants that grow on their own are not cultivated. Cultivating means people prepare the soil and grow the plants on purpose.

items.prompt: What does "cultivate" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Farmers in the valley cultivate rice in flooded fields that they prepare carefully each spring.

options.text: to sell food at a market
to prepare land and grow crops

items.hint: The farmers prepare fields each spring. What are they doing with the rice?
items.explanation: The farmers "prepare" the fields and grow rice in them. Preparing land and growing crops is cultivating.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Our class plans to ___ a small vegetable garden behind the gym, starting by loosening the hard soil.
items.clue: loosening the hard soil; vegetable garden
items.hint: Loosening soil is the first step in what kind of work?
items.explanation: Loosening soil to start a vegetable garden is preparing land to grow plants. That is cultivating. Visiting or photographing a garden does not grow it.

items.prompt: Is this an example of cultivating?
items.passage: Mrs. Ortiz bought a bag of apples at the grocery store and put them in a bowl on her table.
items.hint: Did Mrs. Ortiz prepare land or grow anything?
items.explanation: Buying apples is not growing them. Cultivating means preparing land and growing crops yourself.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what cultivate means.

chunks.text: Early settlers cultivated the prairie
by plowing the thick grass
and planting fields of wheat.
and leaving it untouched forever.

items.hint: Cultivating land means working it to grow crops.
items.explanation: Plowing and planting wheat are the steps of cultivating land. Leaving land untouched is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word best describes what the Inca did on the mountainsides?
items.passage: The Inca built flat steps called terraces into steep mountains, filled them with soil, and grew potatoes and corn there.
items.clue: filled them with soil; grew potatoes and corn
items.hint: They prepared the land and grew food on it.
items.explanation: Building terraces, adding soil, and growing potatoes and corn is preparing land for crops. That is cultivating.

words.definition: a discussion in which people give reasons for different opinions

hero.text: The heroes held a debate about the new rule, with Rex arguing for it and Kai giving reasons against it.

words.everyday: In the class debate, one team argued for a longer recess while the other argued for more library time.

contrast.nonExample: Two friends shouted "Mine!" at each other over the last cookie without giving any reasons.
contrast.explanation: Shouting without reasons is just an argument. A debate is a discussion where each side explains its reasons.

items.prompt: Which situation is a debate?

options.text: Two teams give reasons for and against school uniforms.
A class sings a song together.
A student reads a book quietly at her desk.
Everyone in the room agrees on lunch right away.

items.hint: A debate needs different opinions and reasons.
items.explanation: Two teams giving reasons "for and against" is a debate. When everyone agrees right away, there is nothing to debate.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The town held a public ___ so that people could share their reasons for and against building the new mall.
items.clue: share their reasons for and against
items.hint: Where would people share reasons for and against an idea?
items.explanation: "Reasons for and against" describes a debate. A contest has winners, but it is not mainly about sharing reasons on an issue.

wrong.b: A contest is a competition, but the clue is about sharing reasons on two sides of an issue.

items.prompt: Which word is the OPPOSITE of "debate" in this sentence?
items.passage: After a long debate, the students still could not decide on a name for the class pet.
items.hint: A debate happens because people disagree. What is the opposite of disagreeing?
items.explanation: A debate involves different opinions. Agreement means everyone thinks the same, the opposite. Quarrel is close in meaning to debate, but angrier.

items.prompt: Which word fits best?
items.passage: The two candidates calmly explained their plans and answered questions during the televised ___.
items.clue: calmly explained their plans; answered questions
items.hint: Look for a word that means a calm, organized discussion of different views.
items.explanation: "Calmly explained" and "answered questions" describe an organized debate. A fight or argument sounds angry, and a lecture has only one speaker.

items.prompt: What are the scientists having?
items.passage: Some scientists say the dinosaurs died from a giant asteroid. Others point to huge volcanoes. Both groups share evidence for their view.
items.clue: Some scientists say; Others point to; share evidence for their view
items.hint: Two groups disagree and each gives evidence.
items.explanation: Two groups with different views, each sharing evidence, are having a debate. An experiment tests an idea, but the passage describes people disagreeing.

words.definition: to become smaller, fewer, or weaker over time

hero.text: Pixel noticed the river's fish numbers had declined each year, so the team searched upstream for the cause.

words.everyday: The number of honeybees declined in many areas, which worried farmers who need bees to pollinate crops.

contrast.nonExample: The town's population grew from 5,000 to 8,000 people in ten years.
contrast.explanation: Growing is the opposite of declining. Decline means to get smaller, fewer, or weaker.

items.prompt: Decline can mean "to politely say no" or "to become smaller or fewer". Which meaning is used here?
items.passage: As the forest was cut down, the number of owls living there began to decline.

options.text: to slope downward like a hill

items.hint: Owls cannot say no to anything here. What happens to their number?
items.explanation: "The number of owls" is what declines, so it means became fewer. Owls are not refusing an invitation, so "politely say no" does not fit this sentence.

items.prompt: Which meaning of "declined" is used in this passage?
items.passage: Maya was invited to join the chess club. She thanked the coach but declined because she already had soccer practice.
items.clue: invited; thanked the coach but
items.hint: Maya was invited and thanked the coach. What did she do with the invitation?
items.explanation: Maya "thanked the coach but" did not join, so declined here means politely said no. This is a different sense from the main one you learned: becoming smaller.

wrong.a: That is the meaning for numbers or strength. Here, a person is answering an invitation.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Sales of paper maps have ___ over the years because most people now use phones to find their way.
items.clue: because most people now use phones
items.hint: If people use phones instead, do map sales go up or down?
items.explanation: People using phones instead of maps means fewer maps are sold. Sales declined. Doubled would mean the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is the OPPOSITE of "declined" in this sentence?
items.passage: Grandpa's eyesight declined as he got older, so he needed stronger glasses to read the newspaper.
items.hint: His eyesight got worse. Which word means got better?
items.explanation: Declined here means got weaker, so improved is the opposite. Weakened is a synonym. Refused matches the other sense of decline, which does not fit eyesight.

items.prompt: Which word best describes what happened to the lake's water level?
items.passage: Month after month without rain, the lake shrank. The old dock that once sat in water now stood on dry, cracked mud.
items.clue: the lake shrank; now stood on dry, cracked mud
items.hint: The lake shrank and the dock is now on dry mud.
items.explanation: "Shrank" and the dock on "dry, cracked mud" show the water level dropped over time. That is declining.

words.definition: to add more details to explain an idea fully

hero.text: When the students looked confused, Nova elaborated on her plan, explaining each step and drawing a map.

words.everyday: My teacher wrote "Please elaborate" next to my answer, so I added two examples to support my idea.

contrast.nonExample: When asked why she liked the book, Ana just said, "It was good," and stopped talking.
contrast.explanation: Giving a short answer with no details is not elaborating. To elaborate, you add details and explain more.

items.prompt: Which student elaborates on an idea?

options.text: Ming writes: "Dogs are good pets because they are loyal, playful, and get you outside."
Jake copies the question onto his paper.

items.hint: Look for the answer with added reasons and details.
items.explanation: Ming adds three reasons to explain her idea fully. That is elaborating. Ty states the idea but gives no details.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The scientist's first answer was short, so a reporter asked her to ___ with more details about the discovery.
items.clue: first answer was short; with more details
items.hint: A short answer needs what?
items.explanation: "Was short" and "with more details" show the reporter wanted a fuller explanation. That is elaborating.

items.prompt: Which word is the OPPOSITE of "elaborate" in this sentence?
items.passage: In your essay, elaborate on why the Pilgrims needed help from the Wampanoag during their first winter.
items.hint: Elaborate means to add more. Which word means to make less?
items.explanation: Elaborating makes an explanation longer and fuller, so shorten is the opposite. Describe and explain are close in meaning to elaborate.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what elaborate means.

chunks.text: To elaborate on his point,
Diego added facts about
how much water a leaky faucet wastes.
deleted every detail from his speech.

items.hint: Elaborating means adding, not removing.
items.explanation: Adding facts about water waste gives more detail, which is elaborating. Deleting details does the opposite.

items.prompt: Which line uses "elaborate" naturally?

options.text: "Can you elaborate? I'd like to hear more about why you think that."

items.hint: Which speaker wants more explanation?
items.explanation: Asking someone to elaborate means asking for more detail about their idea, as in "I'd like to hear more". The other lines use the word like wash, drive, or eat.

words.definition: to come out from somewhere or come into view

hero.text: After a long night underground, Rex emerged from the tunnel, blinking in the morning sunlight.

words.everyday: After two weeks inside its chrysalis, the butterfly emerged and slowly spread its wet wings.

contrast.nonExample: The turtle pulled its head back into its shell when the dog barked.
contrast.explanation: Going back inside is the opposite of emerging. To emerge is to come out or come into view.

items.prompt: Is this an example of something emerging?
items.passage: As the fog grew thicker, the tall lighthouse slowly faded until nobody on the beach could see it.
items.hint: Did the lighthouse come into view, or go out of view?
items.explanation: The lighthouse faded out of view. Emerge means the opposite: to come out or come into view.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Every spring, tiny green shoots ___ from the soil where we planted tulip bulbs last fall.
items.clue: from the soil; every spring
items.hint: What do new plants do when they first grow out of the ground?
items.explanation: Shoots coming up "from the soil" are coming out into view. That is emerging. Vanish means the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "emerged" in this sentence?
items.passage: The whale emerged from the deep water, blew a spray of mist, and dove back down.
items.hint: The whale came up out of deep water.
items.explanation: Surfaced means came up to the surface, which matches emerged here. Swam is too general; it does not show coming out into view.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what emerge means.

chunks.text: When the storm passed,
families emerged from their basements
to check on their neighbors.
and stayed hidden inside all week.

items.hint: Emerging means coming out. Which ending shows people out and about?
items.explanation: Coming out of basements to check on neighbors shows emerging. Staying hidden inside contradicts coming out.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the frogs' action?
items.passage: All winter the frogs slept buried in the pond's mud. When the water warmed in April, they climbed out and began to sing.
items.clue: buried in the pond's mud; climbed out
items.hint: The frogs came out from where they had been hidden.
items.explanation: "Climbed out" of the mud after being buried means the frogs came out into view. That is emerged. Escaped suggests getting away from danger or a trap, which isn't the idea here.

wrong.b: Escaped means getting free from danger or a trap. The frogs simply came out when it was warm.
wrong.c: Hibernated describes their winter sleep, not climbing out.

words.definition: to show that something is especially important

hero.text: Kai emphasized the most important safety rule by saying it twice and writing it in giant letters on the board.

words.everyday: The author emphasized the danger of the storm by describing the howling wind in three separate paragraphs.

contrast.nonExample: The coach mentioned the new rule quickly at the end of practice while everyone was leaving.
contrast.explanation: Mentioning something quickly does not show it is important. To emphasize, you make something stand out.

items.prompt: What does "emphasized" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The museum guide emphasized that visitors must never touch the ancient paintings, repeating it at every door.
items.hint: The guide repeated the rule at every door. Why would someone do that?
items.explanation: Repeating the rule "at every door" shows the guide wanted it to stand out as important. That is emphasizing.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: To ___ the key vocabulary, the textbook prints each new word in bold, dark letters.
items.clue: in bold, dark letters
items.hint: Why would a book print words in bold?
items.explanation: Bold letters make words stand out, showing they are important. That is emphasizing. Hiding would be the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "emphasize" in this sentence?
items.passage: In her speech, the principal wanted to emphasize how proud she was of every student.
items.hint: Which word can mean to put extra weight or importance on something you say?
items.explanation: To stress an idea means to give it extra importance, which matches emphasize. Repeating is one way to emphasize, but it does not mean the same thing.

wrong.d: Repeating can be a way to emphasize, but you can repeat something without making it seem important.

items.prompt: Which word fits best?
items.passage: The band played the last note extra loud and long to ___ the dramatic ending of the song.
items.clue: extra loud and long; dramatic
items.hint: Playing a note extra loud makes it stand out.
items.explanation: Playing the note "extra loud and long" makes the ending stand out. That is emphasizing. Mention is too weak, and soften means the opposite.

items.prompt: What is the poster doing with the word "STOP"?
items.passage: The safety poster shows the word STOP in huge red letters, three times larger than any other word on it.
items.clue: huge red letters; three times larger
items.hint: Big red letters make a word stand out.
items.explanation: "Huge red letters" and "three times larger" make STOP the most noticeable word, showing it is the most important. That is emphasizing.

words.definition: completely necessary; something you cannot do without

hero.text: Bolt packed only the essential supplies for the mountain rescue: water, rope, a first-aid kit, and a radio.

words.everyday: Sunlight, water, and air are essential for most plants, which cannot survive without them.

contrast.nonExample: Glitter stickers make Ava's notebook look fun, but she can take notes without them.
contrast.explanation: Something nice to have is not essential. Essential means you truly cannot do without it.

items.prompt: Is the item essential?
items.passage: For a long hike in the desert, Jen brings a fancy hat with a feather that she likes to wear in photos.
items.hint: Could Jen do the hike without the feather hat?
items.explanation: The feather is just for photos; Jen could hike without it. Essential things are completely necessary, like water in the desert.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Calcium is ___ for strong bones, so doctors tell children to eat foods like milk, yogurt, and leafy greens.
items.clue: for strong bones; doctors tell children to eat
items.hint: Doctors want children to eat it. Is it needed or not?
items.explanation: Doctors recommend calcium because bones need it to be strong. Essential means necessary. Optional means you could skip it.

wrong.d: Delicious is about taste. The sentence is about what bones need.

items.prompt: Which word is the OPPOSITE of "essential" in this sentence?
items.passage: Teamwork is essential for building a bridge, since no one person can lift the heavy beams alone.
items.hint: Essential means needed. Which word means not needed?
items.explanation: Unnecessary means not needed, the opposite of essential. Vital means almost the same as essential.

items.prompt: Which word fits best?
items.passage: A key is ___ for opening this lock; without one, there is no way to get the door open.
items.clue: without one, there is no way
items.hint: Helpful and useful mean it makes things easier. Which word means you cannot do it at all without it?
items.explanation: "Without one, there is no way" means the key is absolutely necessary, so essential is the strongest, best fit. Helpful and useful are too weak.

items.prompt: What does the passage show about clean water?
items.passage: When the town's water pipes broke, the hospital could not wash tools or treat patients until trucks brought clean water.
items.clue: could not wash tools or treat patients until
items.hint: What happened to the hospital without water?
items.explanation: The hospital "could not" do its work without clean water, so water was absolutely necessary. That is essential. A luxury is something extra, not needed.

words.definition: to make a careful guess about an amount, size, or value

hero.text: Pixel estimated that the crowd held about 2,000 people by counting one section and multiplying by ten.

words.everyday: Before measuring, Jamal estimated that the classroom was about 30 feet long, and the real answer was 32.

contrast.nonExample: Rosa used a ruler and found that the pencil was exactly 7 inches long.
contrast.explanation: Measuring exactly is not estimating. To estimate, you make a careful, close guess without measuring exactly.

items.prompt: Which student is estimating?

options.text: Lea weighs the pumpkin on a scale: 12 pounds.
Max reads the price tag on a book.
Ana says the jar holds about 200 beans before counting.
Ben counts every bean in the jar one by one.

items.hint: Estimating is a careful guess, not an exact count.
items.explanation: Ana says "about 200" before counting, which is a careful guess. That is estimating. Ben and Lea find exact amounts.

wrong.d: Counting one by one finds the exact number. Estimating is a close guess.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Since we did not have a calculator, Mr. Diaz asked us to ___ the total by rounding each price to the nearest dollar.
items.clue: did not have a calculator; rounding
items.hint: Rounding gives an answer that is close but not exact.
items.explanation: Rounding prices gives a close, careful answer instead of an exact one. That is estimating.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "estimate" in this sentence?
items.passage: Scientists estimate that the oldest tree in the forest is around 3,000 years old.
items.hint: The word "around" tells you the age is not exact.
items.explanation: Approximate means to find a close, not exact, amount, just like estimate. "Around 3,000" shows it is a careful guess. Prove would mean they know for certain.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what estimate means.

chunks.text: Looking at the long line,
Dad estimated
that we would wait about twenty minutes.
that we waited exactly 1,207 seconds.

items.hint: Estimates are close guesses, so they often use words like "about".
items.explanation: "About twenty minutes" is a careful guess, so it fits estimate. "Exactly 1,207 seconds" is a precise measurement, not an estimate.

items.prompt: What is the painter doing?
items.passage: The painter looks at the wall, thinks about past jobs, and says it will probably take about four cans of paint.
items.clue: probably; about four cans
items.hint: Words like "probably" and "about" signal a careful guess.
items.explanation: "Probably" and "about four cans" show the painter is making a careful guess based on experience. That is estimating.

words.definition: to describe something as bigger, better, or worse than it really is

hero.text: Rex exaggerated when he told everyone he had lifted a mountain; it was really just a large boulder.

words.everyday: Tall tales like Paul Bunyan exaggerate on purpose, claiming he dug the Grand Canyon by dragging his axe.

contrast.nonExample: Jess said the fish she caught was ten inches long, and the ruler showed exactly ten inches.
contrast.explanation: Jess described the fish exactly as it was. To exaggerate, you make something sound bigger or more extreme than it is.

items.prompt: Is this person exaggerating?
items.passage: After waiting five minutes for the bus, Owen groaned, "I've been standing here for a million years!"
items.hint: Five minutes or a million years: which is true?
items.explanation: Owen waited five minutes but said a million years. Making something sound much bigger than it is, is exaggerating.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Advertisements sometimes ___ how well a product works, so smart shoppers read real reviews before buying.
items.clue: so smart shoppers read real reviews
items.hint: Why would shoppers need to check real reviews? Ads might make things sound better than they are.
items.explanation: Shoppers check "real reviews" because ads may make products sound better than they truly are. That is exaggerating.

items.prompt: Which word is the OPPOSITE of "exaggerated" in this sentence?
items.passage: The news story exaggerated the damage from the small storm, calling it a disaster when only a few branches fell.
items.hint: Exaggerate makes things sound bigger. Which word means making things sound smaller?
items.explanation: Understated means made something sound smaller or less serious than it was, the opposite of exaggerated. Overstated is a synonym.

items.prompt: Which word fits best?
items.passage: Mom said I ___ when I claimed my little brother "always" takes my toys; he actually did it just once this week.
items.clue: "always"; just once this week
items.hint: It did happen, just not as often as claimed. Is that a total lie, or stretching the truth?
items.explanation: The brother really did take a toy once, so the claim was not completely false. Saying "always" made it bigger than the truth. That is exaggerating, which is different from lying about something that never happened.

wrong.a: A lie is completely untrue. Here something real happened, but it was made to sound bigger.

items.prompt: What is the cartoonist doing?
items.passage: To make people laugh, the cartoonist drew the mayor with ears as big as umbrellas and a nose like a carrot.
items.clue: ears as big as umbrellas; a nose like a carrot
items.hint: Real ears are not as big as umbrellas.
items.explanation: Ears "as big as umbrellas" are much larger than real ears. Making features bigger than they are is exaggerating.

words.definition: unfriendly and ready to fight or oppose

hero.text: The guard robot turned hostile, flashing red lights and blocking the door, until Kai calmly reset its program.

words.everyday: The crowd grew hostile, booing and shouting at the referee after the unfair call.

contrast.nonExample: The new neighbors waved, smiled, and brought over a plate of cookies.
contrast.explanation: Friendly, welcoming behavior is the opposite of hostile. Hostile means unfriendly and ready to oppose.

items.prompt: Which animal is acting hostile?

options.text: A cat purrs and rubs against your leg.
A dog wags its tail and licks your hand.
A rabbit sleeps quietly in its hutch.
A goose hisses and charges at anyone near its nest.

items.hint: Hostile means unfriendly and ready to attack or oppose.
items.explanation: The goose hisses and charges, which is unfriendly, attacking behavior. That is hostile. The cat and dog are friendly.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: For most living things, Antarctica is ___, with freezing winds and almost no liquid water.
items.clue: freezing winds; almost no liquid water
items.hint: Here the word describes a place, not a person. What kind of place makes life hard?
items.explanation: Hostile can describe a place that is harsh and hard to survive in. "Freezing winds" and "almost no liquid water" make Antarctica hostile to life.

wrong.d: Peaceful sounds calm and pleasant, but the clues describe a harsh place.

items.prompt: Which word is the OPPOSITE of "hostile" in this sentence?
items.passage: The two kingdoms had been hostile for years, but the new treaty finally brought them together.
items.hint: Hostile kingdoms are enemies. What is the opposite?
items.explanation: Friendly is the opposite of hostile. Unfriendly is a synonym. Powerful describes strength, not attitude.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what hostile means.

chunks.text: The hostile crowd
booed the speaker
and refused to let her finish.
and gave her a warm welcome.

items.hint: Hostile people are unfriendly. Which ending shows that?
items.explanation: Booing and refusing to let the speaker finish show unfriendly opposition. A warm welcome is the opposite of hostile.

items.prompt: Which word best describes how the shopkeeper treated the boys?
items.passage: When the boys came in, the shopkeeper glared, crossed his arms, and snapped, "Don't touch anything. Get out soon."
items.clue: glared; crossed his arms; snapped
items.hint: Look at his face, his arms, and his voice.
items.explanation: Glaring, crossing his arms, and snapping are unfriendly signals. The shopkeeper was hostile. Nervous would mean worried, not unfriendly.

words.definition: not proud or boastful; not thinking you are better than others

hero.text: Even after saving the city, Juniper stayed humble, thanking the firefighters and saying she was just part of the team.

words.everyday: The humble scientist won a huge prize but said the credit belonged to her students and helpers.

contrast.nonExample: After scoring one goal, Kyle ran around shouting that he was the best player in the whole world.
contrast.explanation: Bragging about being the best is the opposite of humble. A humble person does not show off.

items.prompt: Is this person humble?
items.passage: When her art won first place, Rina smiled and said that many other paintings in the show were just as good.
items.hint: Did Rina brag, or did she give credit to others?
items.explanation: Rina won but praised the other artists instead of showing off. Not boasting about your success is being humble.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Although he was the most famous musician in the country, he remained ___ and never acted more important than his fans.
items.clue: Although; never acted more important than his fans
items.hint: "Although" signals a surprise: he was famous, but how did he act?
items.explanation: "Never acted more important than his fans" describes someone who is not proud. That is humble. Boastful is the opposite.

wrong.c: Wealthy is about money, but the clue is about how he acted toward others.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "humble" in this sentence?
items.passage: The humble champion shook hands with every runner and said she had simply been lucky that day.
items.hint: She didn't brag about winning. Which word means not bragging?
items.explanation: Modest means not bragging about yourself, which matches humble. Shy means nervous around people, which is different: a humble person can be very outgoing.

wrong.c: Shy means nervous around others. The champion shook hands with every runner, so she was not shy, just not boastful.
wrong.d: Arrogant is the opposite of humble.

items.prompt: Which reply is the most humble?
items.passage: Coach: "Great job leading the team to victory today!"

options.text: "Thanks! Everyone worked hard. I couldn't have done it alone."

items.hint: A humble person shares the credit.
items.explanation: Saying "I couldn't have done it alone" shares credit with the team. That is humble. Options a and c are boastful.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the inventor?
items.passage: Reporters called her invention world-changing, but the inventor just shrugged and said she had built on the work of others.
items.clue: just shrugged; built on the work of others
items.hint: How did she react to big praise?
items.explanation: She "shrugged" off big praise and credited "the work of others". Not taking all the credit is being humble.

words.definition: to make an idea clear by giving examples or pictures

hero.text: To illustrate how lightning travels, Bolt drew a zigzag path from the cloud to the tallest tree on the board.

words.everyday: Mrs. Kim illustrated the idea of fractions by cutting a pizza into eight equal slices.

contrast.nonExample: The teacher said "photosynthesis" once and moved on without any example or picture.
contrast.explanation: Just naming an idea does not illustrate it. To illustrate, you use examples or pictures to make it clear.

items.prompt: What does "illustrate" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The author tells the story of one lost puppy to illustrate why animal shelters need more volunteers.

options.text: to draw a picture in color
to make an idea clear with an example

items.hint: The author uses a story, not a drawing. What does the story do for the idea?
items.explanation: The puppy's story is an example that makes the idea clear. Illustrate can mean drawing pictures for a book, but here it means explaining with an example.

wrong.a: Illustrate can mean drawing pictures, but this author uses a story, not a drawing.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: To ___ how the heart pumps blood, our teacher squeezed a water bottle and made water shoot out the top.
items.clue: squeezed a water bottle
items.hint: The water bottle is a model that helps explain something.
items.explanation: Squeezing the bottle is a hands-on example that makes the idea of pumping clear. That is illustrating.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "illustrates" in this sentence?
items.passage: The graph clearly illustrates how the temperature rose each afternoon during the heat wave.
items.hint: A graph does not make the temperature rise. What does it do?
items.explanation: Shows means makes clear, which matches illustrates here. The graph does not cause the heat; it shows it.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what illustrate means.

chunks.text: To illustrate how big the sun is,
Mr. Bell placed a pea next to a beach ball,
so we could compare Earth and the sun.
so nobody could understand anything.

items.hint: Illustrating makes an idea clearer, not more confusing.
items.explanation: The pea and beach ball are an example that helps students compare sizes, which illustrates the idea. Making nobody understand is the opposite.

items.prompt: What is the speaker doing with the story?
items.passage: Talking about honesty, Grandma told how she once returned a wallet full of money and how good it felt afterward.
items.clue: Talking about honesty; told how she once returned a wallet
items.hint: The story is an example of the idea she was talking about.
items.explanation: Grandma's wallet story is an example that makes the idea of honesty clear. That is illustrating her point. She is not drawing anything; illustrate here means explaining with an example.

words.definition: to show or point out that something is true or likely

hero.text: The blinking green light indicated that the bridge was safe, so Kai waved the school bus across.

words.everyday: Dark clouds and a sudden cool wind often indicate that a thunderstorm is on the way.

contrast.nonExample: Liam guessed it would snow tomorrow, even though the sky was clear and the weather report said sunny.
contrast.explanation: Liam's guess had no sign behind it. To indicate is to be a sign that shows something is true or likely.

items.prompt: What does "indicates" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: A fever usually indicates that the body is fighting off some kind of infection.
items.hint: A fever tells you something about what is happening in the body.
items.explanation: A fever is a sign that the body is fighting infection. Indicate means to show or be a sign of something.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The arrows on the museum floor ___ which way visitors should walk to reach the dinosaur hall.
items.clue: arrows; which way visitors should walk
items.hint: What do arrows do?
items.explanation: Arrows point out the way to go. Indicate means to show or point out. Decorate would mean the arrows are just for looks.

wrong.c: Decorate means making something look nice, but these arrows give directions.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "indicated" in this sentence?
items.passage: The survey results indicated that most students would rather have recess before lunch.
items.hint: Results cannot demand anything. What can they do?
items.explanation: Showed means made clear, which matches indicated. Survey results show what students think; they cannot demand or require anything.

items.prompt: What do the clues indicate?
items.passage: The cookie jar is empty, crumbs lead down the hall, and your little brother has chocolate on his chin.
items.clue: crumbs lead down the hall; chocolate on his chin
items.hint: Each clue is a sign. What do they point to?
items.explanation: The crumbs and the chocolate on his chin are signs that point to your brother. They indicate he ate the cookies.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what indicate means.

chunks.text: Rings of salt on the rocks
indicate
that this desert was once covered by a lake.
that nobody knows anything about this desert.

items.hint: Something that indicates gives a clue about what is true.
items.explanation: Salt rings are a sign that water once stood there, so they indicate the old lake. The decoy does not tell what the sign points to.

words.definition: to ask for information about something

hero.text: Pixel called the weather station to inquire about the storm's path before the heroes flew out over the ocean.

words.everyday: My mom stopped at the front desk to inquire about signing me up for swimming lessons.

contrast.nonExample: Theo told his friends all about the movie he saw last night.
contrast.explanation: Telling information is not inquiring. To inquire, you ask questions to get information.

items.prompt: Is this person inquiring?
items.passage: At the zoo, Priya asked the keeper how much food the elephants eat in one day.
items.hint: Is Priya asking for information?
items.explanation: Priya asked a question to get information about the elephants. That is inquiring.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Before planning the trip, Dad wrote to the park office to ___ whether the campgrounds were open in March.
items.clue: whether the campgrounds were open
items.hint: Dad did not know the answer. What was he doing?
items.explanation: "Whether the campgrounds were open" is a question Dad wanted answered. Writing to ask for information is inquiring.

wrong.a: Announcing means telling, but Dad needed to find out something.

items.prompt: Which word is the OPPOSITE of "inquire" in this sentence?
items.passage: Reporters gathered outside to inquire about the cause of the fire at the old factory.
items.hint: Inquire means to ask. What is the opposite of asking?
items.explanation: To inquire is to ask for information, so answer is the opposite. Ask is a synonym.

items.prompt: Which word fits best?
items.passage: The polite customer approached the counter to ___ about the price of the blue bicycle in the window.
items.clue: polite; about the price
items.hint: All four can involve speaking, but which one matches "polite"?
items.explanation: Inquire is a polite, formal way to ask for information. Demand, argue, and shout are too forceful for a polite customer.

items.prompt: In which line is the speaker inquiring?

options.text: "Excuse me, what time does the library close?"

items.hint: Look for the speaker who is asking for information.
items.explanation: Asking what time the library closes is a request for information. That is inquiring. Option a gives the answer instead of asking.

words.definition: to separate something or someone from others

hero.text: Kai built a glass wall to isolate the leaking chemical so it could not spread through the rest of the lab.

words.everyday: The nurse isolated the sick hamster in its own cage so the other class pets would not catch its cold.

contrast.nonExample: The teacher mixed all the groups together so everyone could work with someone new.
contrast.explanation: Mixing everyone together is the opposite of isolating. To isolate means to keep something apart from the rest.

items.prompt: What does "isolate" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Farmers isolate new cows from the herd for a few weeks to make sure they are not carrying any disease.
items.hint: The new cows are kept "from the herd". What does that mean?
items.explanation: The new cows are kept "from the herd" so disease cannot spread. Keeping something apart from others is isolating.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The heavy snowstorm ___ the mountain village for a week, since no cars could reach it.
items.clue: no cars could reach it
items.hint: If nobody can get to the village, what has happened to it?
items.explanation: "No cars could reach it" means the village was cut off from everyone else. The storm isolated it. Connected is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "isolate" in this sentence?
items.passage: Scientists can isolate a single germ from a drop of pond water to study it under a microscope.
items.hint: They want just one germ, apart from everything else in the water.
items.explanation: Separate means to set apart, which matches isolate. The scientists want to study the germ, not destroy it.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what isolate means.

chunks.text: To find the problem,
the electrician isolated one wire
and tested it by itself.
and twisted it together with all the others.

items.hint: Isolating means keeping one thing apart.
items.explanation: Testing one wire "by itself" means it was kept apart from the rest. Twisting it together with the others would be the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word best describes what the ocean did to the island's animals?
items.passage: For millions of years, hundreds of miles of ocean kept the island's birds and lizards apart from animals on the mainland.
items.clue: kept apart from animals on the mainland
items.hint: The ocean kept the animals apart from others.
items.explanation: "Kept apart from animals on the mainland" means the ocean separated them. That is isolating.

words.definition: small or not very important

hero.text: Bolt's suit had only a minor scratch after the rescue, so he fixed it with a dab of paint and kept going.

words.everyday: The story's main character is a girl named June; her cousin is only a minor character who appears once.

contrast.nonExample: The earthquake knocked down bridges and buildings all across the city.
contrast.explanation: Huge, serious damage is not minor. Minor means small or not very important.

items.prompt: Is this a minor problem?
items.passage: Ella's essay was excellent except for one small spelling mistake in the last sentence.
items.hint: Is one small spelling mistake a big deal in an excellent essay?
items.explanation: One small mistake in an excellent essay is not very important. That is a minor problem.

items.prompt: Minor can mean "small or unimportant", "a person under 18", or "a sad-sounding musical key". Which meaning is used here?
items.passage: The movie theater has a rule that a minor must be with an adult to see the late-night horror film.
items.clue: must be with an adult
items.hint: Who would need to be with an adult?
items.explanation: "Must be with an adult" tells you minor here means a young person under 18. This is a different sense from the main one you learned. A worker in a mine is a miner, spelled differently.

wrong.a: That is the adjective meaning. Here minor is a noun naming a person.
wrong.d: That word is miner, which sounds the same but is spelled differently.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The doctor said the cut was ___ and would heal in a few days with just a bandage.
items.clue: heal in a few days; just a bandage
items.hint: A cut that needs only a bandage is big or small?
items.explanation: "Just a bandage" and "a few days" show the cut was small and not serious. That is minor.

items.prompt: Which word is the OPPOSITE of "minor" in this sentence?
items.passage: The new bus schedule caused only minor delays, and most students still arrived before the bell.
items.hint: Minor and its opposite are a common word pair.
items.explanation: Major means large or serious, the opposite of minor. Slight means almost the same as minor.

items.prompt: What does "minor" mean as used in this passage?
items.passage: The two teams agreed on almost everything. They argued only about minor details, like what color the posters should be.
items.clue: agreed on almost everything; like what color the posters should be
items.hint: Poster color is given as an example of the details. Is that a big issue?
items.explanation: The teams "agreed on almost everything", and poster color is a small issue. Minor here means small and unimportant, not young or sad-sounding.

words.definition: to change something a little to make it work better

hero.text: Pixel modified her drone by adding wider wings, which helped it carry medicine to villages in strong winds.

words.everyday: Grandma modified her cookie recipe, using less sugar and adding oats so the cookies would be healthier.

contrast.nonExample: Jake threw away his old model car and bought a completely different one.
contrast.explanation: Replacing something completely is not modifying it. To modify is to make some changes to the same thing.

items.prompt: Which student modified a project?

options.text: Zoe started a brand-new project from scratch.
Tom left his bridge exactly as it was.
Ali added extra supports to his paper bridge so it could hold more weight.
Kim watched a video about bridges.

items.hint: Modifying means changing something you already have, a little, to improve it.
items.explanation: Ali kept his bridge but added supports to make it stronger. That is modifying. Zoe started over instead.

wrong.a: Starting over is not modifying; modifying changes something that already exists.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: When the experiment failed, the scientists decided to ___ one step instead of starting the whole thing over.
items.clue: one step; instead of starting the whole thing over
items.hint: They changed only part of the experiment.
items.explanation: Changing "one step" instead of starting over is making a small change. That is modifying. Repeat means doing the same step again without change.

wrong.d: Repeating the step exactly would not fix the failure. They needed to change it.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "modify" in this sentence?
items.passage: The city plans to modify the old train station so that people in wheelchairs can use it easily.
items.hint: The station will stay, but some parts will change.
items.explanation: Alter means to change something, which matches modify. Demolish would mean knocking the station down completely.

items.prompt: The suffix "-ify" means "to make". "Modify" comes from a Latin word meaning "measure" or "way". Which other word uses -ify the same way?
items.hint: Look for a word where -ify means "to make".
items.explanation: In simplify, -ify means to make (make simple), just as modify means to make something a different way. Family, ivy, and fifty only contain similar letters.

items.prompt: What did the coach do to the game?
items.passage: Because the youngest players got tired quickly, the coach kept the same soccer rules but made the field smaller and the games shorter.
items.clue: kept the same soccer rules but made the field smaller
items.hint: Some things stayed the same, and some changed.
items.explanation: The coach "kept the same soccer rules" but changed the field and game length. Making some changes to improve something is modifying.

words.definition: great in number; very many

hero.text: Nova received numerous thank-you letters from students after she helped rebuild their flooded school.

words.everyday: Numerous stars fill the night sky in the desert, far from the glow of city lights.

contrast.nonExample: Only two students signed up for the chess club this year.
contrast.explanation: Two is a small number. Numerous means very many.

items.prompt: What does "numerous" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The scientist has written numerous books about sharks, filling three whole shelves in our library.
items.hint: The books fill three whole shelves.
items.explanation: Books "filling three whole shelves" means there are a lot of them. Numerous means very many.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The coral reef is home to ___ kinds of fish, from tiny clownfish to giant groupers.
items.clue: from tiny clownfish to giant groupers
items.hint: "From ... to ..." shows a wide range. How many kinds might that be?
items.explanation: "From tiny clownfish to giant groupers" suggests a huge range of fish. Numerous means very many. Few is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is the OPPOSITE of "numerous" in this sentence?
items.passage: Numerous volunteers showed up to clean the beach, and they collected over fifty bags of trash.
items.hint: Numerous means a lot. What means a small number?
items.explanation: Few means a small number, the opposite of numerous. Many is a synonym.

items.prompt: "Numerous" shares a root with "number" and "numeral". The suffix "-ous" means "full of". What does "numerous" most likely mean?
items.hint: Put the parts together: number + full of.
items.explanation: Numer- means number and -ous means full of, so numerous means a great number, very many. It describes amount, not math skill.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the times Emma practiced?
items.passage: Emma practiced her piano piece every morning and every evening for months before the big recital.
items.clue: every morning and every evening for months
items.hint: Twice a day for months adds up to how many times?
items.explanation: Practicing "every morning and every evening for months" adds up to very many times. That is numerous. Rare is the opposite.

words.definition: something that blocks your way or makes it hard to reach a goal

hero.text: A fallen tree was the first obstacle on the path, so Rex lifted it aside and the hikers continued.

words.everyday: Not speaking English was an obstacle for Luis at first, but he practiced every day and made new friends.

contrast.nonExample: The smooth, empty road let the runners go as fast as they wanted.
contrast.explanation: A clear path has nothing blocking it. An obstacle is something that gets in the way.

items.prompt: Is this an obstacle?
items.passage: A big pile of snow blocked the front door, so the family could not get outside to the car.
items.hint: Did the snow get in the family's way?
items.explanation: The snow blocked the door and kept the family from reaching the car. Something that blocks your way is an obstacle.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Lack of money was the biggest ___ to building the new playground, so the town held fundraisers all year.
items.clue: Lack of money; held fundraisers
items.hint: Not having money made building hard. What do you call something that makes a goal hard?
items.explanation: Lack of money stood in the way of the playground, so it was an obstacle. The fundraisers were how the town got past it. An obstacle does not have to be a physical object.

wrong.c: A reason explains why. Here, lack of money is what blocked the goal.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "obstacle" in this sentence?
items.passage: The steep, icy mountain pass was a dangerous obstacle for pioneers traveling west in covered wagons.
items.hint: The pass made the trip harder. Which word names something that blocks the way?
